claims.text: Rapid solvothermal reduction promotes kinetically controlled nucleation of mixed noble-metal atoms.
Kinetically controlled nucleation suppresses phase segregation during nanoparticle formation.
Rapid reduction produces a uniformly mixed high-entropy alloy structure.
A uniformly mixed high-entropy alloy structure hosts abundant and diverse catalytic active sites.
The increased abundance and diversity of active sites enhances catalytic performance relative to nanoparticles made by slower reduction.
A strong reductant, fast heating to 90–150°C, and capping agents can kinetically arrest atomic diffusion.
Rapid reduction triggers simultaneous nucleation of all constituent metal species.
Simultaneous nucleation under rapid reduction outpaces thermodynamically driven atomic diffusion responsible for phase separation.
Kinetic trapping locks in a homogeneous atomic distribution.
A homogeneous atomic distribution provides a high number of catalytically active interfacial sites.
Rapidly reduced nanoparticles will be more homogeneous and single-phase than otherwise identical nanoparticles made by slow reduction.
Rapidly reduced nanoparticles will have at least 20% higher methanol-oxidation turnover frequency than slowly reduced, partially segregated nanoparticles.
Conventional slow reduction permits significant atomic diffusion, causing partial phase segregation and lower catalytic performance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when each noble metal is present at roughly 10–30 at.% and synthesis temperatures are 90–150°C.
Extreme compositions or temperatures outside 90–150°C may produce different formation kinetics and segregation behavior.
